content: Meldonium, also known as Mildronate, THP, MET-88, Mildronāts, or Quaterine, is an anti-ischemic drug that is clinically utilized and manufactured by Grindeks, a pharmaceutical company based in Latvia. It is approved for use in Lithuania and the Russian Federation but is not authorized by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in the United States. Meldonium is clinically employed in the treatment of angina and myocardial infarction. In 2005, the first clinical trial investigating the efficacy of combining meldonium with lisinopril, an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, for the treatment of chronic heart failure was reported. The findings indicated that this combination therapy could enhance the quality of life, exercise capacity, and peripheral circulation mechanisms in patients with chronic heart failure. A subsequent report in 2008 further demonstrated the efficacy of this combination by showing improved carotid baroreceptor reflex in such patients. In February 2010, a clinical trial evaluating the efficacy and safety of meldonium in combination with standard exercise tolerance therapy for angina patients was successfully completed. The results revealed that meldonium significantly improved exercise tolerance in patients with stable angina. Additionally, a Phase II clinical trial on the efficacy and safety of meldonium for acute ischemic stroke was completed in August 2013. The study demonstrated that meldonium was as effective and safe as cinepazide injection. Beyond clinical trials, various scientific research projects have been conducted to enhance the efficacy of meldonium and explore its applicability to other diseases. For instance, a study by Vilskersts et al. suggested that the therapeutic effects of meldonium could be augmented when co-administered with compounds like orotic acid. Animal model studies have shown that meldonium, sometimes in combination with other drugs such as metformin, has beneficial effects on neurological disorders and diabetes. Meldonium may also be effective in treating seizures and alcohol intoxication. Recent reports suggest that meldonium could improve learning and memory by altering the expression of hippocampal proteins associated with synaptic plasticity, as demonstrated in rat models. Meldonium has been reported to elevate the concentrations of γ-butyrobetaine hydroxylase in testicular tissues. Furthermore, long-term administration (90 days) of meldonium has been shown to improve sexual performance, sperm motility, and testosterone levels in boars. However, further studies are required to confirm its potential as an agent for enhancing sperm motility and quality. Currently, meldonium is one of Latvia's most exported pharmaceutical products and is readily available in countries such as Russia, Ukraine, Moldova, Belarus, Azerbaijan, and Armenia. The chemical name of meldonium is 3-(2,2,2-trimethylhydraziniumyl)propionate. It is a structural analogue of γ-butyrobetaine, with an NH group replacing the CH2 group at the C-4 position of γ-butyrobetaine. γ-Butyrobetaine is a precursor in the biosynthesis of carnitine. Meldonium acts as a fatty acid oxidation inhibitor, likely by inhibiting enzymes in the carnitine biosynthesis pathway, such as γ-butyrobetaine hydroxylase. This enzyme, a member of the 2-oxoglutarate (2OG) oxygenase superfamily, catalyzes the formation of L-carnitine from γ-butyrobetaine. X-ray crystallographic and in vitro biochemical studies suggest that meldonium binds to the substrate pocket of γ-butyrobetaine hydroxylase and acts as a competitive substrate/inhibitor. This interaction leads to the formation of malonic acid semialdehyde, dimethylamine, formaldehyde, 3-amino-4-(methylamino)butanoic acid, and (1-methylimidazolidin-4-yl)acetic acid, likely via a Stevens-type rearrangement mechanism. Meldonium is a potent γ-butyrobetaine hydroxylase inhibitor, with a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) value of 62 μM. It serves as an example of a non-peptidyl substrate mimic inhibitor for human 2OG oxygenases. Additionally, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) studies have shown that meldonium binds to carnitine acetyltransferase, an enzyme family critical for cellular energy metabolism. Thus, meldonium may function as a regulator of energy metabolism.
